title: North Sikkim Food: Thukpa, Chhurpi and Lepcha Kitchens
meta_description: What you eat in North Sikkim: lodge dal-bhat, thukpa and momos, yak cheese and butter tea at Thangu, Lepcha millet and greens in Dzongu, cardamom in Mangan.
summary: Food in North Sikkim follows altitude. Lodges in Lachung and Lachen serve rice, dal, vegetables and egg or chicken curry; stalls at Thangu and Yumthang sell Maggi, momos and butter tea. Dzongu homestays cook Lepcha food with millet, nettle and ferns. Mangan grows large cardamom. Most meals cost ₹100–300.

sections.heading: What you will actually eat on a tour
paras: On a shared North Sikkim tour, most of your meals are cooked by the lodge in Lachung or Lachen and are included in the price. Dinner is the same set meal across the valley: steamed rice, dal, one or two vegetables such as cabbage, potato or squash, a pickle, and usually egg curry or chicken for those who eat it. Breakfast is bread and omelette, puri and potato, or noodles, with sweet milk tea. On the Gurudongmar morning the lodge sends you off at 3–4 am with a packed breakfast and a flask of tea.

Lunch on the two drive days is not usually included. Tour vehicles stop at roadside dhabas near Mangan or Chungthang, where a plate of rice, dal and vegetable costs ₹150–250, and chicken or pork adds ₹100–150. It is simple, filling and freshly made. If you are vegetarian, Jain or need a special diet, tell the agent and the lodge before you leave Gangtok; at 2,700 m nobody keeps a large pantry. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood, landslides on the road to Chungthang and Lachen can hold a tour for an extra day, so carry snacks and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Dishes of the high valleys
paras: Lachung and Lachen are Bhutia villages with a Tibetan-style kitchen shaped by cold, yaks and barley. In family kitchens and small cafés you find dishes worth asking for even if the lodge menu does not list them.
list: Thukpa: noodle soup with vegetables, egg or meat, the best thing to eat after a cold day at Yumthang.
Momos: steamed dumplings with cabbage, cheese, chicken or pork, served with a fiery tomato and chilli sauce.
Shaphaley: fried bread pockets stuffed with spiced meat or cabbage, a Bhutia and Tibetan snack.
Thenthuk: hand-pulled flat noodle soup, more common in homes than in lodges.
Chhurpi: cheese made from yak or cow milk, soft and fresh in soup and curry, or rock-hard dried cubes you suck for an hour.
Su cha: salted butter tea churned with yak or cow butter, an acquired taste that helps in the cold.
Tsampa: roasted barley flour mixed with tea and butter, now eaten mostly by older people and at festivals.

sections.heading: Tea stops at Thangu, Yumthang and Zero Point
paras: Above the villages there are no restaurants, only tea stalls run in season by families from Lachen and Lachung. At Thangu, at about 3,900 m, Gurudongmar vehicles stop on the way up and down; the stalls sell sweet tea, coffee, butter tea, Maggi with egg and packets of biscuits. At Yumthang the stalls by the parking area also serve momos and noodles, and at Zero Point, when the road is open, a line of huts sells hot Maggi, tea and soup to people stamping their feet in the snow.

At altitude, eat lightly, drink plenty of warm water and tea, and skip alcohol the night before Gurudongmar. Hot, salty noodles are popular for a reason, but a heavy fried meal before climbing to 5,000 m tends to make altitude sickness worse.

sections.heading: The Lepcha table in Dzongu
paras: Stay in a Dzongu homestay and you eat what the family eats, which is some of the most interesting food in Sikkim. Lepcha cooking relies on what grows around the house and in the forest: rice, maize and finger millet, squash and its shoots, bamboo shoots, wild ferns, stinging nettle cooked into a green soup, mushrooms in season, and fish from the rivers. Meals are lightly spiced, often boiled or steamed, and come with a sharp chilli and tomato relish.

Chi, the fermented millet drink, is part of Lepcha hospitality and ritual. It is served in a bamboo or wooden vessel, topped up with warm water and sipped through a bamboo straw. Hosts offer it to guests, and nobody minds if you take a few sips and leave the rest. If you do not drink alcohol, say so politely; tea is always on the fire.

Ask your hosts to show you the cardamom fields and the drying sheds, and if your stay is long enough, ask to help with a meal. Homestays such as Mayal Lyang in Lingthem have hosted guests for years and are used to explaining what is on the plate.

sections.heading: Large cardamom and other things to take home
paras: Mangan calls itself the large cardamom capital, and from late August through the autumn you smell the pods drying over wood fires in sheds along the road. Large cardamom, the smoky black pod used in garam masala and in meat curries, has been grown under the shade trees of the Teesta valley for generations. In Mangan bazaar it sells for roughly ₹1,500–2,500 a kilo, varying with the market. A 100–250 g packet is a good present.

Other things worth carrying home: dried chhurpi from Lachung and Lachen, which keeps for months; local apples and apple products from Lachung in autumn; dalle khursani, the round, very hot Sikkim chilli, often sold pickled; and Temi tea from South Sikkim, which you will find in Gangtok shops. Buy from village shops and homestays where you can, so the money stays in the valley.

sections.heading: Practical tips for eating well
paras: A few habits make food on this trip easier on your stomach and your budget.
list: Drink boiled or filtered water from your lodge rather than buying plastic bottles; the Dzumsa villages work hard to limit waste.
Carry dry fruit, nuts and chocolate for the long Gurudongmar morning, when the next meal may be five hours away.
Tell the lodge about dietary needs a day ahead, through your agent.
Eat dinner early, around 7 pm, before a 3 am start.
Keep small notes for tea stalls; UPI rarely works where there is no signal.

faqs.q: What food is included in a North Sikkim tour?
faqs.a: Usually dinner and breakfast at the lodge in Lachung or Lachen: rice, dal, vegetables and often egg or chicken curry at night, bread, eggs or puri in the morning, and a packed breakfast for Gurudongmar. Road lunches on the drive days are normally extra, about ₹150–250 for a rice meal.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian food available in Lachung and Lachen?
faqs.a: Yes. The standard lodge dinner of rice, dal and vegetables is vegetarian, with egg or chicken served separately. Momos, thukpa and Maggi come in vegetable versions too. Jain or strictly no-onion food is harder; tell your agent and lodge a day ahead, and carry some snacks of your own.

Chhurpi is cheese made from yak or cow milk, eaten across the Sikkim and Darjeeling hills. Soft chhurpi goes into soups, curries and pickles; dried chhurpi is cut into hard cubes that you chew or suck slowly for an hour or more. Lachung and Lachen sell it in village shops, and it keeps well.

faqs.q: What do Lepcha homestays in Dzongu serve?
faqs.a: Home food made from what grows nearby: rice, maize and millet, squash and its shoots, bamboo shoots, wild ferns, nettle soup, river fish and a chilli and tomato relish. Meals are lightly spiced and included in the homestay price of about ₹1,800–2,500 per person. Chi, the millet drink, is often offered to guests.

faqs.q: Can I get food at Gurudongmar Lake?
faqs.a: Very little. The main food stop is Thangu, at about 3,900 m, where stalls sell tea, coffee, butter tea, Maggi and biscuits. Your lodge in Lachen packs a breakfast for the 3–4 am start. Carry dry fruit, nuts and chocolate, and drink warm water often.

faqs.q: Where can I buy large cardamom in North Sikkim?
faqs.a: In Mangan bazaar, the headquarters town of the district, where shops sell large cardamom for roughly ₹1,500–2,500 a kilo depending on the market. From late August through autumn you can see pods drying in sheds along the road. Small packets of 100–250 g make good gifts.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink alcohol in Lachen before Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Avoid it. Alcohol dehydrates you and makes altitude sickness more likely and worse, and you leave Lachen at 3–4 am for a lake at about 5,180 m. Save the chi or beer for the night after, when you are back down. Drink warm water and tea instead.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for food on a North Sikkim trip?
faqs.a: If lodge dinners and breakfasts are included, about ₹400–700 per person for the whole 3-day tour, covering two road lunches, tea stops and snacks. If meals are not included, budget ₹700–1,000 a day. Dzongu homestays include all meals in the room price.

Chi is the fermented millet drink of the Lepcha people, served in a bamboo or wooden vessel, topped up with warm water and sipped through a bamboo straw. It is part of welcome and ritual, and hosts often offer it to guests. It is fine to take a few sips or to decline politely.
